chunks.text: Four tasks a month. That is the price of a site that never goes stale.

A live restaurant site is not a thing you make once. It is a thing you tend, like the dining room. Four recurring tasks, totaling about ninety minutes a month, keep the site honest, ranked, and trusted. Set them on a calendar today; do them on autopilot from here.

The failure mode of every restaurant website is the same: the operator ships it on Tuesday, feels proud Wednesday, forgets it Friday, and three months later the hours are wrong and the menu still shows the dish they took off in August. Stale sites lose diners faster than no site at all, because diners trust them and then get burned.
What "rhythm" actually means.

Not a vague intention to "keep it updated." A specific set of recurring tasks, with specific frequencies, that you put on a real calendar with a real reminder. Four tasks total. Two of them take ten minutes; one takes thirty; the heaviest takes forty. Total monthly cost: ~90 minutes. Less than the time it takes to count a single Saturday's tip pool.
The point of writing them down is not to remember. It is to not have to remember . The calendar remembers; you just respond to the alert.
A month at a glance.

One example arrangement: hours on the 1st, reviews on the 8th and 22nd (every two weeks), regenerate on the 15th, S E O check on the 30th. Adjust the days to your operator habits, whatever weekday you already do paperwork is the right weekday for these.
The four tasks.

Pick a day-of-week and a time of day right now. "First Monday of the month at 9:30 AM, before service" is a real commitment. "Sometime in early November" is a wish that will not get done. Restaurant operators run on routines, slot these into yours.
Lock it into a calendar.

The widget below builds your monthly rhythm from the four tasks above. Pick a frequency for each (off / weekly / biweekly / monthly / quarterly); the calendar shows where each lands this month. When the cadences feel right, click Download calendar file, a real .ics file lands in your Downloads. Import it into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, or Outlook (most apps open .ics files directly) and the recurring events go live on your phone before you close this tab.
The rhythm does not work until it is on a calendar that wakes you up. Set reminders on your phone for each, 10 minutes before the slot, not 5, so you can finish whatever you are doing first.
When the rhythm breaks (and it will).

Some month you will miss the hours check because Saturday was insane. Some quarter you will skip the S E O check because the dishwasher exploded. That is fine, you are running a restaurant, not a website. The rule is not "never miss." The rule is: when you remember, do the missed task before the new one . The site forgives you. The diners notice the next time you respond to a review or update hours that the lights are still on inside.
What is Not in this bootcamp.

Honest scope-naming. The bootcamp is a complete restaurant-website path, name to deployed site to ongoing rhythm, but it deliberately does not cover four big-and-real adjacent decisions. Knowing what is Not here helps you plan the next quarter intentionally instead of getting frustrated mid-deploy:

Online ordering + delivery integration. Toast TakeOut, ChowNow, Square Online, direct-to-checkout links, these need their own evaluation against your margin model. The bootcamp's L8 (menu) page surfaces dishes; it does not route an "add to cart" flow. If your goal is to escape DoorDash's 30% cut, the most leveraged read is Muntin's DoorDash-math article first, then pick an ordering platform whose economics actually work for your check size.

Reservation widgets (OpenTable, Resy, Tock). Most reservation platforms charge 200 dollars-300/month + a per-cover fee. The bootcamp's L1-generated site has a "Reserve a table" C T A that points wherever you want, phone, email, a Google Form, or a paid widget. The decision of Which platform is not in scope here; the decision of Whether to take reservations is yours.

Gift card sales + e-commerce. Square, Toast, and OpenTable all offer gift card platforms (~3% fee on each sale). A "Gift cards" link in your nav pointing at that platform is two minutes of work, not a lesson. If you sell merchandise (cookbooks, sauces, t-shirts), that is a real e-commerce decision and probably belongs on a separate site or platform.

Email marketing + loyalty programs. Mailchimp, Klaviyo, Square Loyalty, Toast Marketing, all in the 20 dollars-200/month range. The bootcamp captures the operator's G B P and review-response posture; it does not build a Crm. Most independents do not need one in year one; the G B P + a phone number + a personal note to regulars is more than enough for the first 6 months of operations.

None of these block your launch. The site you deployed in L15 plus the rhythm above plus an honest G B P plus 5 regulars writing reviews IS a restaurant marketing system that works for the first six months. Add the four items above only when there is evidence you need them, not because some tool's sales pitch said you should.
A site that stays alive instead of going stale.

Four tasks, ninety minutes a month, set on a calendar today. The hours match reality. The reviews get responses. The site reflects what you actually serve. The S E O catches drift before it costs you anyone. The deployed thing from Lesson 15 stays the asset it became when you shipped it.
Stale sites lose diners. The rhythm is what makes yours not stale.
Print the Lesson 16 tear-sheet →
You finished Open the Doors.

Sixteen lessons. One real, deployed, working restaurant website at a real U R L on your own domain. A response template for the first bad review. Eight S E O phrases that match what your neighborhood actually searches. A 30-day rhythm that keeps all of it true.

The Muntin Method only counts if you ship the artifact. The artifact is yours now, every byte of it lives on a host you control, on a domain you own, with no Muntin lock-in anywhere. We never even saw your data.

If anything in here moved you, share the bootcamp with another operator who is still working from a Squarespace template their cousin set up in twenty seventeen. The next operator who finishes is one more independent restaurant with a site that respects them.
